segments.title: Opening: The Weight of the Vernon Name

utterances.text: Welcome to Hester Unpacked, the podcast that opens up one of the great neglected novels of the Victorian era.
Mrs Oliphant's Hester, published in 1883, is a novel about money, power, and what it costs a woman to be brilliant in a world determined to contain her.
It is also one of the most sharply observed studies of a family institution — the bank, the name, the reputation — that Victorian fiction has to offer.
Today, three exceptional readers join me to take it apart.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than almost anyone alive, and he hears prose the way a musician hears a score — rhythm, timing, and what happens in the silence between the notes.
He brings to Hester the performer's irreplaceable question: what does this sound like when it lives in the air?
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose life's work has been the moral imagination of the Victorian novel.
He reads character as the Victorians themselves did — as the arena where goodness and weakness are tested against circumstance.
Edmund will keep us honest about what the novel is actually doing, as opposed to what we might wish it to be doing.
And Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as maps of class power — he is interested in who owns things, who owes things, and who the system leaves out entirely.
In a novel where the Vernon bank is the beating heart of the community, Daniel is exactly the reader we need.
Let us begin at the beginning — with the name Vernon, the bank, and the extraordinary woman who holds both together.
What strikes me immediately, every time I return to this novel, is that Mrs Oliphant opens with an institution rather than a person.
The Vernon bank is there before Catherine Vernon is — it shapes her, not the other way around.
And then we meet Hester — the young woman who will inherit both the Vernon blood and the Vernon problem.
Oliphant has this extraordinary gift for the image that is also an argument.
She describes Hester's predicament in a single sentence that I find almost unbearable in its compression.

"Between this soft and yielding foundation of her life upon which she could find no firm footing, and the rock of Catherine Vernon who remained quite immovable and uninfluenced by her, coming no nearer as the years went on, yet hemming in her steps and lessening her freedom, the conditions of existence seemed all against the high-spirited, ambitious, active-minded and impatient girl."
Soft and yielding on one side, immovable rock on the other — the girl is not merely constrained, she is geologically trapped.
And that list — high-spirited, ambitious, active-minded, impatient — Oliphant is building a character who should be a hero, not a captive.
Oliver is quite right that the pressure on Hester comes from both directions, and I think that is the novel's central moral geometry.
But I want to attend to Catherine for a moment, because she is the more complex figure, and the more troubling one.
Catherine Vernon is not a villain — she is something far more unsettling than that.
Mrs Oliphant has this devastating passage about the logic of Catherine's self-appointed role in the world.
"When an individual feels capable of performing the part of a visible Providence, it becomes incumbent upon that person, so far as possible, to know everything."
The irony there is exquisite — Oliphant does not accuse Catherine of malice, she accuses her of a perfectly sincere self-delusion.
Catherine genuinely believes she is Providence — and that belief is precisely what makes her so dangerous to those around her.
It is a study in how virtue, or the conviction of virtue, can become the most effective instrument of control.
Edmund locates Catherine's power in her psychology — her self-image as Providence — and that reading is compelling.
But I think we have to ask what material foundation that psychology rests on.
Catherine Vernon controls people because she controls money — and the novel is quite explicit about how that relationship works.
Oliphant gives us this passage about Catherine's attitude toward what she calls the poor relations — and it is worth sitting with what she is describing.
"There was a great deal that was ridiculous in their little affectations and discontents, and the half-resentment, half-exaction with which they received her benefits."
Half-resentment, half-exaction — that is the psychological condition of economic dependency rendered with surgical precision.
The dependants resent the benefactor and simultaneously demand more from her — because what else can you do when someone holds all the economic cards?
And Catherine finds it ridiculous — which keeps her from having to examine the structure that makes her bounty necessary in the first place.
What I love about Daniel's point is that Oliphant earns it completely at the level of the prose.
Half-resentment, half-exaction — that double coinage is not an accident, it is a writer who hears the psychological stutter of the thing.
The people receiving the benefits can't quite land on a single feeling — so neither can the sentence.
That is Oliphant at her most quietly brilliant — the form of the sentence enacts what the sentence describes.
I take Daniel's structural point, though I'd resist reducing Catherine entirely to her economic position.
What is remarkable about Mrs Oliphant is that Catherine's power is not merely purchased — it is earned, and then corrupted.
She saved the bank when the men around her failed — that is the founding act, and it matters morally.
The tragedy is that genuine achievement curdled — over decades — into the need to superintend everyone else's life.
Edmund, I don't deny Catherine's achievement — but the question is what the novel asks us to see alongside it.
Hester inherits the Vernon name but none of the Vernon power — she is the surplus daughter, the one the system has no use for.
And that list Oliver read out — high-spirited, ambitious, active-minded, impatient — every one of those qualities is an economic category as much as a moral one.
Hester has capabilities the system cannot absorb — and so it simply contains her, between the soft yielding mother and the immovable rock.
Contained is exactly the word — and yet Hester is not passive, which is what makes this novel so alive.
In our next segment, we turn to the question of how the novel itself moves — how Mrs Oliphant uses narrative technique to show us what her characters cannot quite say aloud.
The art of evasion — social masquerade and what hides beneath it — is where we go next.

segments.title: The Art of Evasion: Narrative Technique and Social Masquerade

utterances.text: We've been talking about the weight of the Vernon name — the way it shapes every relationship in the novel.
But Mrs Oliphant doesn't just describe that power — she performs it, through a narrative technique of quite extraordinary cunning.
Oliver, you've been itching to get to the narrator — let's start there.
Mrs Oliphant's narrator is one of the great underrated instruments in Victorian fiction.
Not the thundering omniscience of George Eliot, not the arch irony of Thackeray — something more nimble, more conspiratorial.
She takes you by the arm and whispers — did you see what just happened there?
And nowhere is that whisper more devastating than in this passage with Catherine and Edward.
She writes — and you have to let this land —

"What an extraordinary shock would it have been for his companion, who felt herself to sit in the place of the audience, seeing the puppets play their pranks upon the stage and exhibit all their fooleries, to know that she herself was the actor, turned outside in and seen through in all her devices, to this boy whom she loved!"
The audience believes herself the audience — and she is the act.
That reversal is achieved in a single sentence, and it's one of the most quietly thrilling things in the novel.
What strikes me is that Oliphant doesn't use that reversal to humiliate Catherine.
The narrator tells us Catherine is seen through — but the narrator also tells us she is loved, in her way, and that Edward's perception is itself partial.
This is not Swift's savage indignation — it is something more morally generous.
The novel is interested in what it costs a person to be Catherine Vernon — not simply in puncturing her pretensions.
That is the mark of a novelist who understands character as moral fate, not social type.
I'd agree with that — but I'd add that the irony works in both directions, and one of them is entirely social.
Catherine's conviction that she sits above the stage — that she sees clearly while others perform — that's not simply personal vanity.
It's the epistemology of power.
And Oliphant makes this explicit elsewhere — in the passage where Catherine's suspicion of those who won't confide is described.
"Those who were not willing or able to open their hearts, were people who had secrets in their life, and probably a good deal that would not bear the light."
This is the logic of the patron, the employer, the creditor.
Transparency is owed upward — the powerful have the right to know, the dependent have the duty to disclose.
And anyone who withholds — anyone who has an interior life Catherine cannot audit — is morally suspect.
That word — audit — is exactly right, and it connects beautifully to how the narrator handles performance everywhere in this novel.
Because it's not only Catherine who performs — every character is performing for an audience, and the narrator catches them at it.
There's a marvellous little moment with Ashton — Roland Ashton, the charming visitor — that I find absolutely irresistible.
The narrator tells us, with perfect dryness —
"If he had been in the presence of any lady he would have sighed as he said this — being in absolute freedom with one of his own kind he smiled, and it was Edward who sighed."
The performed sigh, withheld; the genuine sigh, accidentally surrendered by someone else entirely.
In twelve words, Oliphant tells us everything about Ashton's social machinery — and everything about Edward's hidden wretchedness.
That sentence is a masterclass in economy.
But I'd want to resist the implication that this makes Ashton simply a fraud.
Oliphant understands — rather in the tradition of Dr. Johnson — that all social life involves performance, and that this is not in itself dishonourable.
What damns a character is not that they perform but what they perform in the service of — selfishness, cruelty, or mere vanity.
The real question Oliphant is pressing, always, is: what is the character beneath the performance?
That's well put — and I think the Vernon sisters illustrate exactly what performance becomes when there's no character beneath it to speak of.
Matilda and Martha Vernon-Ridgway — they exist almost entirely as a social function.
And Oliphant's narrator dispatches them with a single sardonic phrase.
"The sisters immediately plunged into that 'criticism of life' which could scarcely be called poetry, in their hands."
It's a borrowing from Matthew Arnold, of course — criticism of life as the function of poetry — turned on its head.
Their gossip styles itself as cultural judgement while being nothing of the kind.
And what they gossip about — who has money, who has fallen, who is being managed by whom — is the real economy of the novel laid bare.
The Arnold inversion is delicious — Oliphant knew exactly what she was doing.
And it points to something about the way she handles self-deception more broadly.
Because the Vernon sisters don't know they're gossiping — they think they're observing.
And Hester herself is not immune — there's a remarkable passage where Roland manoeuvres her into a feeling she hasn't quite named yet.
The narrator says —
"She was intended to laugh, indeed, if they did not secure another sentiment; but the first aim, and perhaps the last aim, of the insidious Roland, had been to secure this other sentiment."
And then the narrator goes further still —

"Hester did not enter into these distinctions, but she felt them; and when she thus put forward Mrs. Morgan's failing sight, it was with a natural casuistry which she knew would be partially seen through, and yet would have its effect."
She knows she's being slightly dishonest — she knows she'll be caught at it — and she does it anyway, because it will work.
That is not naivety — that is a very sophisticated account of how intelligent people navigate desire.
"Natural casuistry" — that phrase alone is worth the price of admission.
The casuist reasons their way to the conclusion they wished to reach — but Oliphant grants Hester a saving self-awareness.
She is not deceived; she is choosing.
And that distinction — between self-deception and conscious moral compromise — is precisely where Oliphant locates the gravity of Hester's situation.
She is not a fool — she is a person in a situation that makes wisdom very costly.
A person in a situation that makes wisdom very costly — that's a remarkable formulation, and it brings us directly to Hester's mind itself.
Because beneath all this evasion and performance lies a young woman of extraordinary intellectual energy — and a society almost perfectly designed to waste it.
That's where we're going next — Hester's ambition, her hunger, and what the novel makes of a brilliant woman with nowhere to put her brilliance.

segments.title: Hester's Burning Question: Ambition, Class, and the Female Mind

utterances.text: We've been exploring how the novel uses evasion and social performance as narrative strategies.
But beneath all that elegant surface, Hester is burning — with ambition, with frustration, with a hunger that the world around her has no vocabulary for.
What strikes me, returning to the early chapters, is how precisely Oliphant anatomises the formation of Hester's character.
She doesn't simply arrive as a finished type — the ambitious young woman thwarted by circumstance.
She is grown, bent, shaped — almost deformed — by her environment.
The narrator offers what I think is one of the novel's most quietly devastating sentences on this point.
"She came to the flower and bloom of existence with a heart made to believe and trust, yet warped to almost all around, and finding no spot of honest standing-ground on which to trust herself."
That word — warped — is doing extraordinary moral work.
It is not corruption by vice, not weakness of will — it is environmental pressure applied to a nature that was, in itself, sound.
And what Oliphant shows so brilliantly is the feedback loop of that warping.
Because the poison Hester absorbs from the Vernonry — that cutting irony, those little arrows — she then finds herself deploying against the very person she resents.
And here Oliphant gives us a sentence that as a performer I find almost impossible to read without stopping for breath.

"The rage with which she would contemplate herself when she yielded to the first temptation and launched at Cousin Catherine in a moment of passion one of those arrows which were manufactured in the Vernonry, the deep disgust which would fill her when she felt herself, like Catherine, contemplating the world from a pinnacle of irony, chill but smiling, swept her young spirit like tempests."
"Swept her young spirit like tempests."
That is not metaphor as decoration — that is meteorology of the soul.
And then that magnificent throwaway: "To grow at all in the midst of such gales and whirlwinds was something."
I want to hold onto Edmund's word — environment — because the Vernonry isn't simply a moral atmosphere.
It is a specific class formation: impoverished gentility, utterly dependent on Catherine's largesse, producing its cynicism as a defence mechanism.
Hester breathes that air from childhood.
And then Oliphant shows us what that means when she tries to imagine her own ambition — the aspiration to mean something.
There is a passage where Hester articulates her desire for significance with an almost startling nakedness.
"I should like to be a king's daughter or a great soldier's or a great statesman's. I should like my name to mean something. I should like people to say, when they hear it, that is——"
And she can't finish the sentence.
The dash swallows the aspiration whole — because a young woman in her position has no legitimate grammar for what she wants to be.
That is beautifully observed, Daniel — and I would not dispute the material dimension.
But notice what forms of greatness Hester envisions — kings, soldiers, statesmen.
She is reaching for inherited or martial glory — the precisely masculine modes of distinction that her world has built its entire culture around.
This is not merely a class problem — it is a problem of imagination itself, shaped by what models of greatness are available to her.
Oliphant is showing us something tender and almost pitiable here — not because Hester lacks capacity, but because she can only conceive of herself by borrowing male categories of worth.
And then Oliphant places beside that unfulfilled aspiration the bluntest possible constraint: poverty.
There's a moment in Chapter 30 that I find almost cruelly efficient as a piece of prose.

"Her breast swelled, her breath came short with an impulse of impatience and longing to have such an opportunity, to show the mettle that was in her. But how could she do it? Catherine was rich, but Hester was poor."
The body precedes the thought — swelled, breath came short — and then the mind catches up with the brutality of the situation in a single flat sentence.
"Catherine was rich, but Hester was poor." Eight words.
Oliphant doesn't reach for a metaphor there — she doesn't need one.
That sentence is doing the work of a whole chapter of Victorian moralising — and doing it without a syllable of pity.
What Oliphant understands — and this is where she is more radical than she perhaps intended — is that virtue without resources is not virtue, it is aspiration with no traction.
Hester has the mettle Catherine once had — but Catherine had capital behind that mettle.
And then there is that even more searching question Hester poses much later, which strikes me as the novel's moral spine.

"Was it natural, then, a thing she could accept as just, that it was enough for her to sympathise, to share the consequences, to stand by the chief actor whatever happened, but never to share in the initiative or have any moral concern in the motive or the means of what was done?"
That is not a woman bemoaning her lot.
That is a philosophical proposition about the structure of moral life — about who gets to be an agent and who is permanently cast as witness.
The question is genuinely Burkean in its structure — not a demand for revolution, but a plea for just recognition within an existing order.
She is not asking to overturn the world — she is asking whether the world, as constituted, is defensible.
"Never to share in the initiative" — that phrase cuts.
Because throughout the novel we watch Hester possessed of exactly the initiative that the men around her squander.
The irony is the point — and Oliphant is too careful an artist to make it easy.
And
the men around her who do possess the initiative — Edward above all — are about to demonstrate exactly how catastrophically they can misuse it.
Which brings us, rather urgently, to Edward himself — and to the question of what he does with all that freedom of action Hester is denied.
His gamble, and the economics of desperation that drive it, are waiting for us next.

segments.title: Money Moves: Edward's Gamble and the Economics of Desperation

utterances.text: We've been talking about Hester's ambition and the ways the novel frustrates it — but there's another character whose ambition takes a far darker turn.
Edward Vernon: speculator, embezzler, and one of Victorian fiction's most unsettling studies in what happens when a man of feeling discovers money.
What strikes me first about Edward is how clearly Oliphant understands that speculation isn't just a financial act — it's a psychological one.
She gives us this extraordinary passage where Edward watches the money market with something approaching religious awe.
"The blowing of the winds and their changes were prose compared to the headlong poetry of the money-market."
Poetry. She reaches for the Romantic vocabulary deliberately.
Because the money market doesn't just tempt Edward — it transfigures him, in the way that sublime experience is supposed to transfigure the poet.
And Oliphant knows exactly how dangerous that is — when capital starts to look like art, the moral faculty simply switches off.
And she tracks the switching-off with forensic precision.
There's a line that I find genuinely chilling, and I've read a great deal of chilling Victorian prose.

"His mind had gone further than his practice, and had reached a point of excitement at which the boundaries of right and wrong become so indistinct as to exert little, if any, control over either the conscience or the imagination."
Notice what she's doing there — it's not that Edward chooses evil.
The categories themselves dissolve. Right and wrong become a kind of fog.
That's a much more disturbing account of moral collapse than simple wickedness would be.
I think Oliphant is doing something more classical than either of you are allowing.
Edward is a study in what the moral tradition calls akrasia — weakness of will.
He knows, at some level, what he is doing. The confession he makes to Hester is remarkably clear-eyed.
"Suspicion produces treachery, don't you know? I cannot be true here. No, don't say anything. I ought, but I cannot. It is in the air."
"I ought, but I cannot" — that is not the speech of a man who has lost the categories of right and wrong.
That is the speech of a man who sees the good and turns away from it — which is, if anything, the older and the more tragic portrait.
But Edmund, the atmosphere Edward describes isn't merely personal weakness — it's structural.
He says "it is in the air" — all of them making believe and finding each other out, yet going on all the same.
That's a description of an institution — the bank, the family, the whole apparatus of respectability — held together by mutual performance of sincerity that nobody actually feels.
And the most damning detail is what Edward finds when he opens that black bag.
"He was looking over them now with the greatest care, and a face full of suppressed, but almost solemn excitement.
They were securities of all kinds, and meant an amount of money which went to Edward's head even more than the chances of fortune."
The securities themselves are intoxicating — not what they might buy, but what they represent: accumulated, abstracted, socially legitimised power.
And nobody is watching. That's the truly gothic element of the scene.
Oliphant gives us the thought that goes through Edward's mind as he handles those papers — and it's an extraordinary piece of psychological horror dressed in perfectly calm prose.
"All that in his power; no chance of being called upon to produce them, or to render an account of the stewardship which had been so freely committed to him!
It was enough to make any man's head go round."
"Any man" — she doesn't exonerate him, but she does universalise the temptation.
The trust itself becomes the corruption. The more freely it was given, the more devastating it is to abuse.
There's a passage earlier in the novel where Edward reflects on the appeal of financial ruin that I find almost scandalously candid.
"A man requires a great deal of original impulse before he will go the length of murder.
The other has a milder but similar attraction; you ruin other people, which shakes them up, and gives a change of air."
The breezy nonchalance of "a change of air" is what makes it land so hard.
Oliphant is not letting Edward off the hook — she is showing us precisely how the self-justifying mind works, with pitiless accuracy.
And yet when the crisis finally arrives, what Edward cannot face is not prosecution — it's the return to ordinariness.
That line is the most revealing thing in the whole arc.
"Had there been only the risks of the crisis, the meeting of alarmed and anxious creditors, the chance even of criminal prosecution, he might have faced it;
but to return again to that old routine, to take up his former life, was impossible."
Prison he could perhaps endure. Subordination — dependence on Catherine's goodwill — that he cannot.
What breaks Edward isn't greed in the simple sense — it's the intolerable smallness of the life that awaited him if he failed.
And Oliphant gives his ruin exactly the tempo it deserves — which is to say, no dramatic cataclysm, just a slow, remorseless current.
She writes: "The course of events went on in that leisurely current which is far more deadly in its sweep than any sudden cataract."
Leisurely. That word does all the work.
Because Edward expected drama — a great coup, a decisive moment — and instead he got time.
Time in which to accumulate danger without quite noticing it, like a man walking slowly into deep water.
And there's one final flourish to Edward's disgrace — a companion on his flight from England whose identity Oliphant withholds from Catherine, and from us, with almost satirical timing.
She calls it simply "the most wonderful complication of all" — and moves on, with the precision of someone who knows exactly how much silence is worth.
That quality — the irony, the perfectly placed withholding — takes us directly to what we want to explore next: the wit and the darker humour that run through the whole fabric of Middleton society.

segments.title: Wit, Irony, and the Darker Corners of Middleton

utterances.text: We've been tracing the financial tremors running through Middleton — Edward's gamble, Catherine's exposure, the whole edifice shaking.
But Mrs Oliphant never lets the darkness go unlit by irony, and this segment is about the wit — and the something darker beneath it.
The thing that keeps striking me about Catherine Vernon is that she's genuinely funny — and the narrator knows it.
She has been running a private theatre in her own drawing room for years — watching her dependents perform, noting every hypocritical smile, every suppressed resentment.
And the narrator gives us the whole machinery of it in one extraordinary sentence.

"She did not desire to be turned from the comedy which she had in her way enjoyed for years, seeing through, as she said, all the little world of dependents that hung about her, drawing out their weaknesses, perceiving the bitter grudge that lay under their exterior of smiles."
That phrase — 'as she said' — is doing tremendous work.
It's the narrator slipping a tiny blade between Catherine's ribs — gently noting that this is Catherine's version of herself, not necessarily the truth.
You're right to catch that, Oliver — the indirection is masterly.
But I'd go further and say Mrs Oliphant is diagnosing something morally precise here — not merely comic.
Catherine has made a deliberate choice not to examine herself — she prefers the entertainment of others' failings to the uncomfortable mirror of her own.
The sentence goes on — and this is the crucial turn — to acknowledge what she refuses to recognise.
"—in order to turn to what might prove the less amusing contemplation of her own weaknesses, or recognise the element of evil in that which was certainly not amusing."
'The element of evil.' That is not a phrase Mrs Oliphant uses lightly.
She is telling us that Catherine's comedy — her whole way of being in the world — has a moral cost she will not pay.
And the material structure underneath that comedy is worth naming.
Catherine's entertainment depends entirely on her dependents' humiliation — and the narrator makes that explicit.
The phrase is 'the humiliation of being in her debt' — debt is the engine of the whole performance.
Catherine can only watch the comedy because she holds the financial power that compels these people to perform.
Remove the debt, and the theatre closes.
Which is precisely what Edward's catastrophe brings about — and it's why that financial crisis is also a kind of existential one for Catherine.
And we see that existential rupture rendered physically — almost gothically — in the scene where Catherine and Hester face each other after the crash.
The setting is extraordinary — it's dawn, but the shutters are still closed, candles still burning.
Listen to what Mrs Oliphant does with that room.

"The windows were all closed, and candles upon the table still burning: but the light swept in from above, over the top of the shutters, and lighted up the room in a strange abstract way like a studio or a prison."
A studio or a prison — she holds both possibilities in the air simultaneously.
Art and confinement — the two things Catherine has made of her life, in one image.
That image carries the whole weight of the novel's irony, I think.
Catherine built the Grange as an expression of her independence — and now the very room that housed her sovereignty becomes something spectral, suspended between night and day.
The 'strange abstract' light is perfectly chosen — abstract is the word for what her world has become: stripped of the concrete relationships and obligations that gave it form.
And then — and this is what I find most remarkable — she simply refuses to grieve it.
Which is where that later passage becomes so strange and unsettling.
Catherine is about to lose the Grange — the entire material apparatus of her power — and the narrator tells us she feels virtually nothing about it.
The line Mrs Oliphant gives us is almost breathtaking in its cool register.
"Had she been actually brought down as far as the almshouse, in all likelihood she would have taken it with the proudest placidity."
'The proudest placidity' — that is a portrait of a woman who has so thoroughly identified with her own will that the material conditions barely touch her.
Which is extraordinary, but it's also a kind of pathology — the system that made her powerful has become so internalised that even its destruction leaves her unmoved.
There's also something comic in it — the sheer nerve of the woman.
The narrator asks, with perfect deadpan: 'What was there in that to move a soul?'
And you can't quite decide whether Catherine is magnificent or terrifying — or both.
That's the particular genius of this novel — Mrs Oliphant never resolves it for you.
Magnificent and terrifying — and utterly alone with that knowledge.
Which brings us precisely to where we need to go next: what it costs Catherine to be the only person in Middleton who truly sees — and what that isolated clarity finally means for her.

segments.title: The Burden of Knowledge: Catherine Alone in Her Power

utterances.text: We've been exploring the irony and social comedy that runs through the world of Middleton — but beneath that wit, there is a much darker current.
This segment, I want to turn to Catherine Vernon herself — to what it costs a woman to hold power, and to hold it alone.
What strikes me, every time I return to these later chapters, is how Oliphant earns her tragedy.
She doesn't announce it. She doesn't underline it in red.
She lets Catherine stand outside in the early summer dawn and simply — look up.
The passage is so spare it almost disappears, which is exactly why it destroys you.
Listen to what Oliphant actually writes — she says:
"Her eyes, under the curve of pain, which makes the eyelids quiver, looked up to the pale skies with what is the last appeal of humanity."
The last appeal of humanity. Not Catherine's appeal — humanity's.
In four words, Oliphant lifts one woman's broken night into something universal. That is a novelist at full stretch.
Oliver is quite right, and I think we should sit with that image rather than rush past it.
What Oliphant is doing there is something very old — the question of theodicy, of why suffering falls on the virtuous.
And she gives it to Catherine in terms that are almost liturgical in their plainness.
The passage reads:
"An honest life, an honourable career, a soul that had shrunk from no labour or pain, a hand that never had been closed to human distress — and repaid with misery at the end."
Three parallel clauses, each one a credential — and then that devastating turn: repaid with misery.
And then the question that follows — I find it among the most searching lines in the novel:
"Is there no reason in it when God's creature lifts a face of anguish to His throne, and asks why?"
Oliphant does not answer the question. She doesn't soften it. She leaves it open, which is an act of extraordinary moral courage in a Victorian novelist.
I want to honour the weight of that reading, Edmund — and then complicate it slightly.
Because Oliphant doesn't just ask why suffering falls on the virtuous in the abstract.
She is very precise about the specific economy of Catherine's suffering — who took from her, and who gave nothing back.
There's a passage in chapter forty where the narrator anatomises Catherine's entire adult life in a single sentence, and it is merciless:
"Everyone around had taken from her, and snarled at her, eaten of her bread, and drunk of her cup, and hated her — except Edward."
Eaten of her bread, drunk of her cup — those are biblical cadences, but Oliphant is also giving us a ledger.
A precise accounting of extraction. Catherine has been the bank, the larder, the source — and the household has fed on her and despised the hand that fed.
And then Edward — the one exception, the one who returned devotion — turns out to have been taking in a different and more ruinous way.
The structure of the betrayal is the structure of the whole novel: power without reciprocity becomes its own annihilation.
What I keep returning to is the question of knowledge — of who in the novel actually sees what is coming.
Because Oliphant gives us this remarkable passage about Hester — not Catherine — sensing disaster before it arrives.
And the image she reaches for is volcanic:
"There were not even any heavings and groanings, like those that warn the surrounding country before a volcano bursts forth."
No warning. No theatrical tremor. And yet Hester knows.
Oliphant tells us she feels it — and here is the phrase that stops me every time — through
"the keen sight of injured pride and wounded feeling, seeing the secret thread of meaning that ran through everything."
The secret thread of meaning. Hester reads the world precisely because she has been pushed to its margin — exclusion has sharpened her vision.
There's something almost unbearable in that — because the knowledge earns her nothing, changes nothing, saves no one.
I think that's precisely the moral geometry Oliphant is tracing.
Catherine wields power — genuine, earned, formidable power — and it isolates her absolutely.
Hester is excluded from power — and that exclusion becomes, paradoxically, the condition of her clearest sight.
But Oliver is right — sight without agency is its own form of imprisonment.
Both women are trapped — one by the burdens of her power, the other by the denial of it.
And Oliphant, to her great credit, refuses to privilege either fate. She regards them both with the same steady, anguished clarity.
And what haunts me is that Oliphant shows us this system grinding on — and the novel's ending offers no structural remedy.
Catherine's question — why? — is addressed to heaven. But Oliphant's novel asks it of the social order.
An honest life, an honourable career — Catherine's virtues are real. And they count for nothing against the capacity of those around her to take.
That's not a question for God. That's a question for an economic arrangement that places one woman at the centre of accumulation and calls it family.
Catherine at the threshold of her desolate house, Hester sensing the thread no one else can see — Oliphant holds both women in focus simultaneously, and it is devastating.
Which brings us, I think, to the hardest question the novel poses: what, finally, does Hester get to have — and what remains permanently beyond her reach?

segments.title: Closing: What Hester Teaches Us—And What She Cannot Have

utterances.text: We've been sitting with Catherine's loneliness at the height of her power — that terrible isolation that comes from knowing too much and trusting too little.
Now I want to turn to what this novel ultimately leaves us with — what Hester is given, and what she is denied.
What strikes me, coming back to the novel as a whole, is how consistently Oliphant gives Hester the right instincts and then withholds the stage.
There's a passage that I think is the emotional heart of the book — not a dramatic scene, just a flare of interior longing.
Oliphant writes of Hester's craving —

"a desire which many a young mind has felt as well as Hester; to have that golden opportunity — the occasion to do a heroic deed, to save some one, to venture your own life, to escape the bonds of every day, and once have a chance of showing what was in you!"
"Once have a chance of showing what was in you."
That's the whole tragedy in a subordinate clause.
It is a remarkable passage — and Oliphant's use of that word "bonds" is not accidental.
She is not simply describing frustrated ambition — she is naming a universal condition of youth, male or female.
What gives the passage its weight is that it does not become a polemic about women's exclusion.
Oliphant generalises to "many a young mind" — and in doing so, she deepens rather than diminishes the particular injustice.
Hester's predicament becomes more poignant, not less, for being shared.
I'd push back slightly on that reading — or rather, press it further.
The desire is universal, yes — but the bonds are not equally distributed.
Hester has the intelligence, the nerve, the moral seriousness — everything required for heroic action.
What she lacks is access — structural, financial, gendered access to the machinery by which such action becomes possible.
The novel knows this, even if it can't quite say it outright.
And that gap — between what the novel perceives and what it can articulate — is where the real politics of the book live.
And then there is Catherine's death — which is, I think, one of the most quietly devastating things Oliphant ever wrote.
It doesn't thunder. It doesn't even announce itself.
Listen to how Oliphant renders it — the whole scene is built from light and silence and a single physical detail.
"Her pale head against the dark curtains stood out like ivory. Some time afterwards she sighed two or three times heavily, then there was no sound at all."
"A chill crept into the room like nothing Hester had ever felt before, though all was still, serenely warm and bright to outward appearance."
"Serenely warm and bright to outward appearance."
That's a sentence of absolute genius.
It is the technique of the true moralist — to let the horror reside entirely in the gap between surface and reality.
The fire burns. The lamp glows. The book sits open.
And the woman who built an empire out of sheer will has simply — stopped.
But I think one must hold this against what Oliphant showed us of Catherine's interior state in the chapters before.
She had written of Catherine — and I find this quite shattering — that she faced a darkness that would never be dispersed.
"Her last stronghold had fallen. This it is which makes calamity so terrible to the old. She could not get beyond it."
"She could not get beyond it."
Three words that demolish every illusion about the consolations of age.
What I keep returning to is the juxtaposition Oliphant engineers between those two women in that room.
Catherine has had everything — authority, resources, the power to shape lives.
Hester has had almost nothing — her intelligence, her pride, and her position as permanent supplicant in Catherine's house.
And here they are: the powerful one dying in her chair, the dependent one sitting beside her with a book she cannot read.
The system produces this — not as tragedy but as routine.
One woman exhausted by power, one woman exhausted by its absence.
And yet the novel doesn't leave Hester crushed — there's a stubborn vitality in her that survives everything the plot throws at her.
That desire for the golden opportunity — Oliphant doesn't extinguish it.
She leaves it burning, unanswered, at the end.
Which is either a counsel of despair or an act of extraordinary honesty — probably both.
I should say — and I mean this with full sincerity — that this novel has reminded me why Mrs. Oliphant deserves to be read with the seriousness we give to her contemporaries.
She is not a minor talent rescued from obscurity.
She is a major writer who has been allowed to fall from our attention — and that is an indictment of our attention, not of her work.
What strikes me finally is that Hester herself has no resolution.
The question the novel poses from its first pages — what is a woman of this quality to do with herself in a world that will not make room for her — remains unanswered at the last.
And that is not a failure of nerve on Oliphant's part.
It is the most honest thing she could have done.
I think that's exactly the right note to end on — a novel that refuses to be tidier than the world it describes.
We began today with Catherine Vernon at the height of her power and her loneliness, and we've ended with Hester — still waiting, still burning, the golden opportunity still just out of reach.
My warmest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Dr. Daniel Rosen — three readers who have brought this remarkable novel back into the light it deserves.
And to you, listening — thank you for spending this time with Hester and with us.
She has earned far more than the afternoon.

Between this soft
and yielding foundation of her life upon which she
could find no firm footing, and the rock of Catherine
Vernon who remained quite immovable and uninfluenced
by her, coming no nearer as the years went

against the high-spirited, ambitious, active-minded
and impatient girl, with her warm affections, and
quick intelligence, and hasty disposition.

c13:p2.text:
When an individual feels capable of
performing the part of a visible Providence, it
becomes incumbent upon that person, so far as
possible, to know everything, to shut his eyes to no
detail, to note every little incident, and to encourage [Pg 203] 
not only the confidences of his possible clients and
 protégés , but the observations of all surrounding them,
and every hint as to their motives, their intentions
and purposes, that can be got at.

c13:p2.best_quote: When an individual feels capable of performing the part of a visible Providence, it becomes incumbent upon that person, so far as possible, to know everything.

c7:p8.text:
It cannot be denied that this was to some
extent the tone unconsciously adopted by Catherine
in her dealings with the poor relations who were so
largely indebted to her bounty. There was a great
deal that was ridiculous in their little affectations
and discontents, and the half-resentment, half-exaction
with which they received her benefits.
c7:p8.summary: The ridiculous affectations of the poor relations could have made Catherine misanthropic, but instead cultivated cynicism and contemptuous tolerance.

c17:p91.text:
What an extraordinary shock
would it have been for his companion, who felt
herself to sit in the place of the audience, seeing
the puppets play their pranks upon the stage and
exhibit all their fooleries, to know that she herself
was the actor, turned outside in and seen through
in all her devices, to this boy whom she loved!
c17:p91.summary: The narrator delivers a brilliant ironic revelation: Catherine believes herself the audience observing the foolish actors of her little world, but is actually the actor being observed and judged by Edward, whom she loves.
c17:p91.best_quote: What an extraordinary shock would it have been for his companion, who felt herself to sit in the place of the audience, seeing the puppets play their pranks upon the stage and exhibit all their fooleries, to know that she herself was the actor, turned outside in and seen through in all her devices, to this boy whom she loved!

c13:p3.text:
The outside crowd,
knowing nothing of the meaning of these investigations,
is apt to mistake them altogether; but
Catherine did not care much about the outside world. It was her wish that everything should be told her,
and she was perhaps too apt to think that those who
were not willing or able to open their hearts, were
people who had secrets in their life, and probably a
good deal that would not bear the light.
c13:p3.summary: Catherine dismisses the outside world's judgment and assumes anyone unwilling to confide in her must be hiding something shameful.
c13:p3.best_quote: Those who were not willing or able to open their hearts, were people who had secrets in their life, and probably a good deal that would not bear the light.

c19:p29.text:
"I don't think that is my experience. My old
people are very indulgent; but then, I am a mere
visitor. Home does not mean much to me," said
Ashton. If he had been in the presence of any lady
he would have sighed as he said this—being in
absolute freedom with one of his own kind he smiled,
and it was Edward who sighed.
c19:p29.summary: The narrator notes that Ashton would perform melancholy for ladies but reveals his true indifference with Edward, whose sigh betrays his contrary emotional depth.
c19:p29.best_quote: If he had been in the presence of any lady he would have sighed as he said this—being in absolute freedom with one of his own kind he smiled, and it was Edward who sighed.

c29:p38.text:
The sisters immediately plunged
into that "criticism of life" which could scarcely be
called poetry, in their hands.
c29:p38.summary: The sisters are about to engage in gossip, which the narrator sardonically describes as criticism.
c29:p38.best_quote: that 'criticism of life' which could scarcely be called poetry, in their hands

c21:p100.text:
She
was intended to laugh, indeed, if they did not secure
another sentiment; but the first aim, and perhaps
the last aim, of the insidious Roland, had been to [Pg 79] 
secure this other sentiment. Hester did not enter
into these distinctions, but she felt them; and when
she thus put forward Mrs. Morgan's failing sight, it
was with a natural casuistry which she knew would
be partially seen through, and yet would have its
effect.
c21:p100.summary: The narrator explains that Roland's true aim beneath the humor was to secure genuine romantic sentiment, and that Hester deployed conscious casuistry in her defense, knowing it would be partially transparent yet effective.

c8:p13.text:
It was not
to be expected that she could grow otherwise than
contorted with the blasts. She came to the flower
and bloom of existence with a heart made to believe
and trust, yet warped to almost all around, and
finding no spot of honest standing-ground on which
to trust herself.
c8:p13.summary: Hester enters young adulthood with a capacity for belief but warped by her corrupting environment, unable to find solid moral ground.
c8:p13.best_quote: She came to the flower and bloom of existence with a heart made to believe and trust, yet warped to almost all around, and finding no spot of honest standing-ground on which to trust herself.

c8:p12.text:
The rage with which she would
contemplate herself when she yielded to the first
temptation and launched at Cousin Catherine in a
moment of passion one of those arrows which were
manufactured in the Vernonry, the deep disgust
which would fill her when she felt herself, like
Catherine, contemplating the world from a pinnacle
of irony, chill but smiling, swept her young spirit
like tempests. To grow at all in the midst of such
gales and whirlwinds was something.
c8:p12.summary: Hester's self-reproach for moments of cruelty to Catherine and adoption of Catherine's cynicism sweeps over her like violent storms, causing deep psychological turmoil.
c8:p12.best_quote: The rage with which she would contemplate herself when she yielded to the first temptation and launched at Cousin Catherine in a moment of passion one of those arrows which were manufactured in the Vernonry, the deep disgust which would fill her when she felt herself, like Catherine, contemplating the world from a pinnacle of irony, chill but smiling, swept her young spirit like tempests.

c23:p104.summary: Hester confesses her desire for achievement and renown: to be born to greatness or to earn her own significance.
c23:p104.best_quote: I should like to be a king's daughter or a great soldier's or a great statesman's. I should like my name to mean something. I should like people to say, when they hear it, that is——

c30:p91.text:
Her breast swelled, her breath came short with an
impulse of impatience and longing to have such an
opportunity, to show the mettle that was in her. But how could she do it? Catherine was rich, but
Hester was poor. In this way she was diverted for
the moment from her anxiety.
c30:p91.summary: Hester's desire to act heroically is constrained by her poverty, which denies her the resources Catherine possessed.
c30:p91.best_quote: Her breast swelled, her breath came short with an impulse of impatience and longing to have such an opportunity...But how could she do it? Catherine was rich, but Hester was poor

c36:p91.text:
Hester kept gazing through that wintry blackness,
with eyes still wide open, and her clear brows
puckered with wonder and alarm. Was it natural,
then, a thing she could accept as just, that it was
enough for her to sympathise, to share the consequences,
to stand by the chief actor whatever happened,
but never to share in the initiative or have [Pg 125] 
any moral concern in the motive or the means of
what was done?
c36:p91.summary: Hester questions whether women's prescribed role—to sympathize and share consequences but never to understand or influence the action—is just or natural.
c36:p91.best_quote: Was it natural, then, a thing she could accept as just, that it was enough for her to sympathise, to share the consequences, to stand by the chief actor whatever happened, but never to share in the initiative or have any moral concern in the motive or the means of what was done?

c25:p58.text:
It was not for this sort of trifling work
that he had set himself to watch those fluctuations,
which are more delicate than anything in nature
they could be compared to. The blowing of the
winds and their changes were prose compared to
the headlong poetry of the money-market. Edward
felt so many new pulses waking in him, such a
hurrying fever in his veins, that he could not control
himself.
c25:p58.summary: Edward feels awakening excitement at the delicate fluctuations of the money market, which he compares to poetry rather than prose.
c25:p58.best_quote: The blowing of the winds and their changes were prose compared to the headlong poetry of the money-market.

c32:p3.text:
And, indeed, his
mind had gone further than his practice, and had [Pg 24] 
reached a point of excitement at which the boundaries
of right and wrong become so indistinct as to
exert little, if any, control over either the conscience
or the imagination.
c32:p3.summary: Edward's mental state has reached dangerous heights where moral boundaries have become blurred and ineffective.
c32:p3.best_quote: his mind had gone further than his practice, and had reached a point of excitement at which the boundaries of right and wrong become so indistinct as to exert little, if any, control over either the conscience or the imagination

c29:p31.text:
"You could do nothing less: but I cannot be
different here. Suspicion produces treachery, don't
you know?" he said, with his face close to her ear. "I cannot be true here. No, don't say anything. I ought, but I cannot. It is in the air. All of us,
every one except you, we are making believe and
finding each other out, yet going on all the same.
c29:p31.summary: Edward confesses his inability to be true to himself under Catherine's watch, describing the pervasive atmosphere of insincerity and suspicion she creates.
c29:p31.best_quote: I cannot be different here. Suspicion produces treachery, don't you know? I cannot be true here. No, don't say anything. I ought, but I cannot. It is in the air. All of us, every one except you, we are making believe and finding each other out, yet going on all the same.

c32:p76.text:
The papers he was
examining he had brought himself in a black bag
from the safe in the bank. He had locked the black
bag into an old oak escritoire till after dinner. He
was looking over them now with the greatest care,
and a face full of suppressed, but almost solemn
excitement. They were securities of all kinds, and
meant an amount of money which went to Edward's
head even more than the chances of fortune.
c32:p76.summary: Edward examines securities stolen from the bank safe with suppressed excitement, intoxicated by the amount of money they represent.

All [Pg 37] 
that in his power; no chance of being called upon to
produce them, or to render an account of the stewardship
which had been so freely committed to him! It
was enough to make any man's head go round.
c32:p77.summary: Edward realizes that as a trusted steward of the bank's securities, no one will question his management, and this absolute power intoxicates him.
c32:p77.best_quote: All that in his power; no chance of being called upon to produce them, or to render an account of the stewardship which had been so freely committed to him! It was enough to make any man's head go round

c19:p31.text:
"A
man requires a great deal of original impulse before
he will go the length of murder. The other has a
milder but similar attraction; you ruin other people,
which shakes them up, and gives a change of air."
c19:p31.summary: Edward elaborates that bankruptcy, though milder than murder, offers similar appeal—it disrupts others' lives and provides the excitement of upheaval.
c19:p31.best_quote: A man requires a great deal of original impulse before he will go the length of murder. The other has a milder but similar attraction; you ruin other people, which shakes them up, and gives a change of air.

c39:p44.text:
Had there been only the risks of the crisis, the
meeting of alarmed and anxious creditors, the chance
even of criminal prosecution, he might have faced it;
but to return again to that old routine, to take up
his former life, was impossible. He flew along like
the wind. There was still an hour or more before
the train would start. Would the women gather
themselves together, he wondered, soon enough to
send after him, to prevent his journey?
c39:p44.summary: Edward reflects that he might have faced financial ruin and prosecution, but cannot bear to return to his ordinary former life; he resolves to walk to the train junction.
c39:p44.best_quote: Had there been only the risks of the crisis, the meeting of alarmed and anxious creditors, the chance even of criminal prosecution, he might have faced it; but to return again to that old routine, to take up his former life, was impossible.

c37:p29.text:
In this way the spring went on. It had appeared
to Edward himself as certain that some great  coup 
must have settled his fate long before. It was his
inexperience, perhaps, and the excitement of his
determination to act for himself, which had made
everything appear so imminent; but after all it did
not turn out so. The course of events went on in
that leisurely current which is far more deadly in its
sweep than any sudden cataract.
c37:p29.summary: Edward's financial ventures proceed gradually and indecisively, with neither clear gain nor catastrophic loss, but slow accumulation of danger.
c37:p29.best_quote: The course of events went on in that leisurely current which is far more deadly in its sweep than any sudden cataract.

c44:p20.text:
The most wonderful complication of all, the companionship
in which he had left England, was not
told to her then. It threw to all the others a
horrible mockery upon the whole story.
c44:p20.summary: The narrator hints at a remarkable discovery: Edward's companion in his departure from England, a detail kept from Catherine initially.
c44:p20.best_quote: The most wonderful complication of all, the companionship in which he had left England, was not told to her then.

c17:p74.text:
She did not desire to
be turned from the comedy which she had in her
way enjoyed for years, seeing through, as she said, all
the little world of dependents that hung about her,
drawing out their weaknesses, perceiving the bitter
grudge that lay under their exterior of smiles, and
the thousand ways in which they made up to themselves
for the humiliation of being in her debt—in
order to turn to what might prove the less amusing
contemplation of her own weaknesses, or recognise
the element of evil in that which was certainly not
amusing.
c17:p74.summary: The narrator reveals Catherine's determination not to turn from her enjoyment of observing others' weaknesses and self-interest, preferring not to examine her own nature or recognize the evil in her judgement.

c41:p21.text:
The
windows were all closed, and candles upon the table
still burning: but the light swept in from above, over
the top of the shutters, which were not so high as the
glass, and lighted up the room in a strange abstract
way like a studio or a prison.
c41:p21.summary: The room is lit by a strange mixture of candlelight and dawn light, creating an abstract, prison-like or studio atmosphere.
c41:p21.best_quote: The windows were all closed, and candles upon the table still burning: but the light swept in from above, over the top of the shutters...lighted up the room in a strange abstract way like a studio or a prison.

c45:p2.text:
She showed no feeling
about it, people said; and indeed Catherine felt
that neither about this nor any other external thing
was she capable of showing much feeling. She cared
nothing about leaving the Grange. Had she been
actually brought down as far as the almshouse, in all
likelihood she would have taken it with the proudest [Pg 259] 
placidity. What was there in that to move a soul?
c45:p2.summary: Catherine shows no sentiment about leaving the Grange or selling its contents, viewing material possessions as inconsequential to a person of her philosophical temperament.
c45:p2.best_quote: Had she been actually brought down as far as the almshouse, in all likelihood she would have taken it with the proudest placidity.

c41:p2.text:
It was scarcely
one o'clock, but in summer there is little night, and
already the air had begun to whiten with some premonition
of day. She held up her face to the sky—an
old face, with so many lines in it, suddenly [Pg 198] 
smitten as with a death-blow. Her eyes, under the
curve of pain, which makes the eyelids quiver, looked
up to the pale skies with what is the last appeal of
humanity.
c41:p2.summary: As dawn breaks, Catherine lifts her aged, grief-stricken face to the paling sky in a gesture of ultimate human appeal and anguish.
c41:p2.best_quote: Her eyes, under the curve of pain, which makes the eyelids quiver, looked up to the pale skies with what is the last appeal of humanity.

c41:p3.text:
For why?—for why?—an honest life, an
honourable career, a soul that had shrunk from no
labour or pain, a hand that never had been closed to
human distress—and repaid with misery at the end! Is there no reason in it when God's creature lifts a
face of anguish to His throne, and asks why? She
paused on the threshold of her house, which was
desolate, and made that mute appeal.
c41:p3.summary: Catherine's unspoken lament questions divine justice: after a lifetime of honest, laborious virtue and compassion, why is she repaid with misery?
c41:p3.best_quote: Is there no reason in it when God's creature lifts a face of anguish to His throne, and asks why?

c40:p30.text:
Through Catherine's mind at that moment there ran
the whole story of her later days, how she had used
herself to the pretences of all about her, how every
one around had taken from her, and snarled at her,
eaten of her bread, and drunk of her cup, and hated [Pg 186] 
her—except Edward. He alone had been her prop,
her religion of the affections.
c40:p30.summary: Catherine's entire adult life has been consumed by serving others who exploited her; only Edward seemed to reciprocate her devotion.
c40:p30.best_quote: everyone around had taken from her, and snarled at her, eaten of her bread, and drunk of her cup, and hated her—except Edward.

c31:p132.text:
There were not even any heavings
and groanings, like those that warn the surrounding
country before a volcano bursts forth. Nevertheless,
this girl, who had been so long a spectator, [Pg 22] 
pushed aside from the action about her, but with
the keen sight of injured pride and wounded feeling,
seeing the secret thread of meaning that ran
through everything, felt premonitions, she could not
tell how, in the heated air, and through the
domestic calm.
c31:p132.summary: The narrator eloquently describes Hester's sensitive perception of imminent crisis; despite outward calm, she senses approaching danger like a volcano about to erupt, perceiving hidden meaning beneath surface tranquility.
c31:p132.best_quote: All was still, and everything going on in its calm habitual way. There were not even any heavings and groanings, like those that warn the surrounding country before a volcano bursts forth. Nevertheless, this girl, who had been so long a spectator, pushed aside from the action about her, but with the keen sight of injured pride and wounded feeling, seeing the secret thread of meaning that ran through everything, felt premonitions, she could not tell how, in the heated air, and through the domestic calm.

c30:p92.text:
The question as to
how the bank came into that peril, the suspicion
that her father must have been somehow connected
with it, the heat of her research after the key of the
mystery, faded away for the moment in a vague,
general excitement and eager yet vain desire to have
it in her power to do something, she also——a
desire which many a young mind has felt as well
as Hester; to have that golden opportunity—the
occasion to do a heroic deed, to save some one, to
venture your own life, to escape the bonds of every
day, and once have a chance of showing what was in
you!
c30:p92.summary: Hester's yearning for the heroic opportunity to transcend her limited circumstances distracts her from anxiety about her father.
c30:p92.best_quote: a desire which many a young mind has felt as well as Hester; to have that golden opportunity—the occasion to do a heroic deed, to save some one, to venture your own life, to escape the bonds of every day, and once have a chance of showing what was in you!

c45:p30.text:
And the silence resumed its sway. She laid
herself back as before—her pale head against the
dark curtains stood out like ivory. Some time
afterwards she sighed two or three times heavily,
then there was no sound at all. The fire burned
cheerfully, the lamp shed its steady glow upon
Hester's book, to which after this talk she did not,
as may be supposed, pay very much attention.
c45:p30.summary: Catherine lays back with her pale head against dark curtains and becomes still. Hours pass as Hester reads, then a supernatural chill sweeps through the warm room as Hester realises Catherine's hands have grown cold.
c45:p30.best_quote: her pale head against the dark curtains stood out like ivory. Some time afterwards she sighed two or three times heavily, then there was no sound at all... A chill crept into the room like nothing Hester had ever felt before, though all was still, serenely warm and bright to outward appearance.

c43:p4.text:
Her last stronghold had fallen. This it
is which makes calamity so terrible to the old. She
could not get beyond it. There was nothing, nothing
in her path but this, blocking it across with a darkness
that would never be dispersed. If he had died
she would have known she could not remain long
behind him, and the gloom would have been but a
mist between; but he had not died.
c43:p4.summary: Catherine's final defences have crumbled; she faces a darkness that ageing offers no comfort in escaping, unable to imagine endurance.
c43:p4.best_quote: Her last stronghold had fallen. This it is which makes calamity so terrible to the old. She could not get beyond it.
